CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right heel pain, radiating up into the calf, while training for a triathlon.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Dennis is a new patient who is training for a triathlon. He reports pain in the back of the right heel that extends up into the calf. The pain occurs typically after a workout and when he first gets up in the morning. On first getting out of bed the area feels very tight and "almost like it's tearing." It eases somewhat after walking for about 10 to 15 minutes. It becomes sore again if he sits for an extended period and then gets back up, and also after a lot of activity. The pain is mainly in the right leg, not the left.

Training: He runs about 10 km in the morning, bikes 45 minutes to 1 hour at lunchtime, and swims 30 minutes to 1 hour in the evening. He trains five days a week. On weekends he alternates between a long run and a long bike ride, with no long swim, and takes one day off. He does not stretch at all because he has no time. On the bike he starts slowly until warmed up. The doctor did not ask about prior medication use but assumed that whatever he had been doing was not working significantly.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right heel and calf pain and tightness as per HPI. No left leg pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Lower extremities:
- Dorsiflexion of the right foot and ankle produces mild pain.
- Resisted movement produces mild pain.
- Calf squeeze (Thompson test): no pain with squeezing of the left or right calf. The doctor stated the Thompson test is negative.
- Squeezing the right heel causes significant pain.
- Palpation up the right Achilles tendon is very tender.

RESULTS
No imaging performed. X-ray is not indicated at this time.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Achilles tendinitis, right, from overuse in the setting of aggressive triathlon training.
- Stop training for 1 to 2 weeks to allow healing.
- Ibuprofen (Advil) 3 tablets every 6 hours as an anti-inflammatory.
- Physical therapy referral for a couple of visits for strengthening and instruction in stretching before activity.
- No x-ray at this time.
- Follow up in 7 to 10 days, after the first couple of physical therapy appointments, to monitor progress. The patient should call the office to schedule once physical therapy is arranged.
- If he still has significant pain without change at about 10 days despite activity modification, more aggressive treatment options may be considered.
- The patient agreed with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up of chronic problems: depression, hypertension, and status post rotator cuff repair.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Edward is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history significant for depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair who presents for follow-up of his chronic problems. He reports the last six months have gone well.

Depression: At the last visit he was considering new strategies for managing his depression and did not want to start medication because he is already on multiple medications. He now sees a counselor once a week and has been swimming at the pool frequently this summer and fall. He feels his depression is going well and does not feel the need for medication at this time. He knows he can call if that changes.

Hypertension: He was struggling with blood pressure control six months ago. He reports good days and bad days. He takes his medication (Norvasc) daily. He admits that burgers, wine, and salt occasionally sneak into his diet. He checks his blood pressure about once a week at a CVS pharmacy machine.

Rotator cuff repair: The repair was done about eight months ago. He reports it is doing well. He stretches with a yoga ball and is getting stronger each time. He has progressed from physical therapy to home exercises, which he can continue once a week.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No complaints reported.
HEENT: Denies nasal congestion.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain. Reports ankle swelling, mainly near the end of the day, that resolves by the next morning.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 156/94, elevated. Recent home and pharmacy readings have been running a little high over the past couple of months.
Cardiovascular: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously noted and stable.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Extremities: 1 to 2+ pitting edema in the legs.

RESULTS
Labs: Reviewed and look good. Creatinine (kidney function) is stable.
EKG: Normal. No evidence of coronary artery disease.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
59-year-old male with depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair presenting for follow-up.

1. Depression: Well managed with weekly counseling, swimming, and a good support system. No medication needed at this time. He may call if he feels he needs to start medication.

2. Hypertension: Not well controlled. Blood pressure was 156/94 today, with recent readings running high. Lower extremity edema may be related to salt intake. Increase Norvasc to 10 mg daily. Order an echocardiogram and a lipid panel. Discussed diet and decreasing salt intake.

3. Status post rotator cuff repair: Doing well and essentially resolved. Continue home exercises. No further intervention needed.

The patient had no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and peripheral vascular disease. The patient also reports foot and leg discomfort.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Maria Martin, DOB 03/05/1946, presents for follow-up. She consented to recording of the visit. She reports feeling "pretty good" overall.

Diabetes: She received the letter about her last results showing poorly controlled sugars, with an A1c of 9.9. She had not increased her glimepiride as instructed and is still taking 2 mg. She had just filled the prescription. She is also on metformin. Diet: she is not eating much pasta or bread. When she has bread it is wheat, usually two slices in the morning, and occasionally a peanut butter sandwich. She hardly drinks soda and drinks club soda or seltzer water instead of regular water.

Eyes: Eye exams are up to date and she recently got new glasses. She sees the group on Liberty Road, where the doctor changes each visit, and previously saw Dr. Sanchez. She had cataract surgery and waited about a month to heal before getting her prescription. She is not happy with the lens in one eye, which she says feels odd, while the other eye is good.

Hypertension: A home blood pressure reading a couple of weeks ago was 116. She reports taking metoprolol 50 mg daily, lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg daily, and amlodipine 10 mg daily.

Hyperlipidemia and vascular disease of the legs: She is on atorvastatin and tolerating it. She reports her feet "feel like hell" all the time, her legs bother her, and she cannot walk much. She also has pain up to the hips, involving the hips and upper legs. She is trying to walk.

Tobacco: She is still smoking and is not ready to quit, but says she will think about it.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Eyes: Vision improved after cataract surgery, but she is unhappy with the lens in one eye.
Respiratory: Recent cough with congestion, producing relatively clear sputum. The cough improved this morning. No shortness of breath.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain, pressure, or tightness.
GI: No nausea, vomiting, or GI symptoms.
GU: Slower urinary stream, which she describes as stable. Urinates several times per day. Nocturia only occasionally. She tends to drink her beverages in the evening.
Musculoskeletal: Pain in the legs, hips, and upper legs. Limited walking.
Neurologic: Foot discomfort. No headaches or dizziness.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Carotids normal, no bruits.
Cardiovascular: Regular rhythm, normal rate, crisp S1 and S2, no murmurs.
Lungs: Clear, no rales or wheezing.
Extremities: No edema. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable.
Feet: Thickened nails. Mildly dry skin with no skin breakdown. Mildly decreased sensation at the tips of the first and second toes.
Blood pressure: 140/60 on recheck in clinic.

RESULTS
Previous A1c was 9.9. Labs were not yet available at this visit.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Type 2 diabetes, poorly controlled (A1c 9.9)
- Increase glimepiride. She should take two of her 2 mg tablets twice daily until the new prescription is filled, then one 4 mg tablet twice daily.
- Continue metformin.
- Watch for hypoglycemia (weak, shaky, sweaty) and notify the office if it occurs.
- Recheck labs today.
- Encouraged cutting down on bread and continuing to avoid sugary drinks.

2. Hypertension
- Clinic BP 140/60, with better home readings. Continue metoprolol 50 mg daily, lisinopril/HCTZ 20/25 mg daily, and amlodipine 10 mg daily.
- Check kidney function today.

3. Hyperlipidemia and peripheral vascular disease
- Continue high-dose atorvastatin to protect the arteries.
- Symptoms are relatively stable. Encouraged continued walking.

4. Peripheral neuropathy, mild
- Keep feet moisturized.
- A medication is available if symptoms worsen, but she is already on many medications. She may use a foot cream or scrub.

5. Status post cataract surgery
- She is unhappy with one lens. The eye clinic may offer laser cleanup, and she will see what they say.

6. Tobacco use
- Advised to quit. She is not ready, but will think about it.

7. Cough and congestion
- Lungs clear on exam and the cough is improving. No specific treatment discussed.

Follow-up: Labs today. Return in 4 months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after an emergency room visit for shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Louis is a 58-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure who presents for follow-up after an ER visit. On Saturday he was playing tennis in very hot, humid weather. After about half an hour he became very short of breath and had difficulty breathing. He thought he was having a heart attack and became very nervous. His wife took him to the ER, where everything "checked out." About six hours after returning home he felt very lightheaded and dizzy. On Sunday he felt fine. He wanted to follow up.

He reports being very diligent with his heart failure medications and is in touch with his doctor. He tries to avoid junk food and salty foods but admits he cheats every now and then, though he has mostly done well.

He had a cataract removed from his eye three months ago and reports no problems or vision changes since. He had a skin cancer removed about five months ago, which healed nicely with no problems since.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: Shortness of breath and difficulty breathing during tennis on Saturday.
Neurological: Lightheadedness and dizziness about six hours after returning home from the ER on Saturday; resolved by Sunday.
Eyes: No vision problems.
Skin: Skin cancer excision site healed without problems.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure mildly elevated. The ER report also noted elevated blood pressure.
Neck: Supple. No jugular venous distention.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmur.
Respiratory: Fine crackles bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema in both legs.

RESULTS
ECG: Stable for the patient. Shows left ventricular hypertrophy.
Echocardiogram: Pumping function of the heart is mildly reduced but stable.
Skin biopsy pathology: Skin cancer was fully removed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Shortness of breath, likely heart failure exacerbation (congestive heart failure) due to dietary indiscretion with salty food causing fluid retention. Exam shows fine bibasilar crackles and trace bilateral lower extremity edema, consistent with extra fluid. ECG is stable with left ventricular hypertrophy, and echo shows stable, mildly reduced pumping function on appropriate medical therapy.
- Prescribe extra dose of Lasix 80 mg once a day.
- Start carvedilol 25 mg twice a day.

2. Elevated blood pressure. Noted today and in the ER. Doctor stated this will need to be discussed further.

3. Status post cataract removal. Doing well with no vision problems. No medication adjustment needed.

4. Status post skin cancer removal. Healed well, and pathology shows complete removal. No medication adjustment needed.

The nurse will see the patient shortly.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lower back pain after an injury about four months ago.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jeremy injured his lower back about four months ago while moving boxes during his son's move out of a college dorm. At the time of injury, he felt a brief sensation of being unable to support his upper body weight, and the toes of his right foot tingled for about an hour. The tingling resolved and has not recurred. He reports leg weakness only when carrying something heavy, and he is nervous about lifting. He still has intermittent sharp low back pain with certain turns or when rolling over in his sleep, which resolves with repositioning. He tried physical therapy at his gym without benefit. He has taken Tylenol and ibuprofen and has tried heat and ice, with little relief. Ibuprofen helps slightly more than Tylenol but for a shorter duration. He has had no stomach upset from ibuprofen. He went to urgent care, where an MRI was recommended. He did not get it because of insurance concerns and because he was starting to feel better. Because symptoms have persisted, he now wants to proceed with the MRI. He denies bladder or bowel problems, incontinence, difficulty urinating or defecating, fever, and chills.

Past medical history: total right knee replacement in spring 2020, with good recovery (about 95% function).

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Genitourinary: No bladder incontinence or difficulty urinating.
Gastrointestinal: No bowel incontinence or difficulty with bowel movements. No stomach upset with ibuprofen.
Musculoskeletal: Intermittent low back pain. Leg weakness with heavy carrying.
Neurological: Right toe tingling at time of injury, resolved. No ongoing numbness or tingling.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: No fever. Blood pressure 117/56. Heart rate 68. Oxygen saturation 95% on room air.
Neck: Bony protuberance appreciated at C5-C6. No pain to palpation.
Lumbar spine: No pain to palpation. Decreased flexion and extension. Positive straight leg raise. Spasm of the paraspinal muscles.
Musculoskeletal: Lower extremity strength equal bilaterally.

RESULTS
Lumbar spine x-ray: No acute bony abnormality and no fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute lumbar disc herniation, suspected based on persistent symptoms after the injury. The bony prominence at C5-C6 may reflect arthritis in the neck, and the back findings may reflect residual injury.
- Order lumbar spine MRI to evaluate soft tissue, as x-ray shows only bone.
- Refer to physical therapy through the health system.
- Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg once daily.
- If a herniated disc is confirmed, other options such as an epidural steroid injection could be discussed to reduce inflammation.
- The patient had no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain and swelling after dropping a landscape brick on the foot.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Elijah is a patient referred by his primary care provider after dropping a landscape brick on his right foot yesterday while doing yard work. He reports the foot is sore today. Immediately after the injury it was sore, but he kept working and moving around on it. The foot has since become swollen, which prompted him to see his primary care doctor. He has been "lucking it up" and has not taken any medications such as Tylenol or ibuprofen for the pain because he prefers not to take medicine. He rates his pain currently as 11 out of 10. He reports the whole foot is numb and says it has been numb for a long time.

Past history: About 20 years ago he broke his ankle and was treated with a cast. It generally does well, but it occasionally becomes sore and swells. He also reports that his other ankle is sometimes sore, that he has had surgery on it, and that it may give out once in a while. He is unsure whether these are related to the current injury.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right foot pain and swelling. Occasional soreness and swelling of the prior ankle fracture site. Occasional soreness of the other ankle, which may give out.
Neurological: Numbness of the whole right foot, reported as longstanding.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Look good per physician.
Right foot: Bruising on the plantar and dorsal aspects of the foot. Swelling present. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot.
Neurovascular: Capillary refill brisk, less than 3 seconds. Strong bounding dorsalis pedis pulse. Motor and sensation intact. Findings are symmetric bilaterally.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot: Dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal, 3 mm separation between the bases of the first and second metatarsals, and presence of bony fragments.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right Lisfranc fracture (second metatarsal base, midfoot), with associated swelling and bruising.
- Order MRI of the right foot to assess for ligamentous injury. Outpatient MRI facility is on site, and the MRI can be done this afternoon.
- Surgery is likely needed, using plates and screws to realign the bones and allow bones and ligaments to heal properly. Poor alignment or ligament healing could lead to loss of the arch, flatfoot deformity, and arthritis.
- Surgery is outpatient (same-day), proposed for tomorrow. The patient would be discharged home that evening.
- Follow-up 24 hours after the procedure, then again at 2 weeks.
- Postoperative care: cast and crutches, non-weight-bearing for 6 to 8 weeks, with gradual advancement of ambulation based on healing and tolerance.
- The patient asked about staying in a cast without surgery. The physician explained that this is possible, but the best outcomes come from alignment with plates and screws.
- The patient asked to think about the surgery, and the physician agreed. The nurse will complete paperwork and set up the procedure if he agrees.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Elevated and fluctuating blood pressure.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Thompson is a 67-year-old male with a history of essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. His blood pressure has normally been very well controlled. Over the last 3 to 4 weeks he has had periods of lightheadedness and slight headache. His systolic blood pressure has occasionally been over 180, higher than any prior readings. He has checked his blood pressure both when feeling fine and during lightheaded episodes, and readings during the episodes have been on the high side. He has not passed out recently. He reports occasional mild chest heaviness that is not sustained. He denies respiratory or breathing difficulty. He feels a little unsteady when dizzy and has a slight headache when his blood pressure is higher. He describes the dizziness as feeling "fuzzy" and lightheaded, not spinning. He denies fever, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He denies palpitations usually.

Medications: lisinopril 20 mg twice daily (increased from once daily at the last visit). He very rarely misses doses. He uses a pillbox and has tried a medication reminder app, which was confusing to set up, but he reports staying on schedule accurately. He also takes atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia.

Osteoarthritis: Mostly controlled. He is able to golf most of the time but sometimes plays less or skips a day when the weather changes. He takes Tylenol for mild pain and modifies activity as needed.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever.
Cardiovascular: Occasional mild chest heaviness, not sustained. Denies palpitations usually. No recent syncope.
Respiratory: Denies breathing difficulty.
Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.
Neurologic: Lightheadedness ("fuzzy"), slight unsteadiness with dizziness, slight headache with higher blood pressure. No spinning sensation.
Musculoskeletal: Mild osteoarthritis pain, weather-related.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior.
Respiratory: Mild bibasilar rales. No wheezes or rhonchi. Excellent air movement.
Extremities: Trace bilateral lower extremity edema.
Other: Remainder of exam otherwise normal and unremarkable.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Essential hypertension, uncontrolled with fluctuating readings
- Increase lisinopril to 60 mg twice daily.
- Add hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.
- Check blood pressure twice daily for the next 2 weeks.
- Follow up in 2 weeks.
- Counseled to stay well hydrated with 6 to 8 glasses of water per day, more with warm weather or increased activity.
- Counseled to limit alcohol to no more than a couple of drinks per week given fluctuating blood pressure.

2. Hyperlipidemia
- Continue atorvastatin.
- Order cholesterol panel, CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis (to assess kidney function).

3. Osteoarthritis
- Continue to stay active without overdoing it, including walking and golfing.
- Tylenol as needed for mild pain.

Heart murmur: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur is unchanged from prior; will continue to monitor.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Joint pain, mainly in both knees.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Janet is a 33-year-old female who presents with bilateral knee pain. She has been doing more stair-type workouts, which she thought would build muscle and help her knees, but her knees have been bothering her instead. The pain affects both knees equally. She denies pain in other joints such as the elbows or shoulders. She had a right rotator cuff repair about two years ago and has had no problems since.

She has diabetes and reports her blood sugars have been under control. She has hypertension and takes Norvasc 5 mg daily, taken every day. She monitors her blood pressure at home, and it has not been elevated since the joint pain began.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever or chills.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain. Denies leg swelling.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea or vomiting.
Musculoskeletal: Bilateral knee pain. Denies elbow or shoulder pain.
Neurological: Denies pins and needles in the feet.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure is elevated today. The doctor noted the patient may be nervous.
Neck: Soft, no thyroid enlargement.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Abdomen: Soft.
Musculoskeletal: Left knee with slight erythema and edema and a small effusion. Decreased flexion and extension of the left knee. Lower extremity strength is good.

RESULTS
Left knee x-ray: Normal.
Labs: White blood cell count not elevated. A1c is mildly elevated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left knee pain, possible knee strain. X-ray is normal and WBC is not elevated, so infection is not a concern.
- Send an autoimmune profile to work up the left knee pain.
- Refer to physical therapy.
- Start meloxicam 15 mg once daily for pain and inflammation.

2. Hypertension. Blood pressure is elevated today, possibly from nervousness.
- Continue Norvasc 5 mg daily.
- Continue to monitor blood pressure at home. The patient has a cuff. She will send a report of readings in the next couple of weeks.
- Order a lipid profile.

3. Diabetes. A1c is mildly elevated but not terrible.
- Continue metformin 500 mg twice daily.

The patient had no further questions and agreed with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Pain in the distal arm near the wrist (distal radius) after a tennis injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mrs. Martinez is a 43-year-old female who presents with pain in her arm toward the wrist, in the area of the distal radius. The pain began after she was playing tennis. While hitting a backhand, she missed the ball and struck the pole of the net, which jarred her arm. She reports a small amount of swelling, not a lot. She has a little pain when she moves her wrist. She denies numbness in her hand.

Past medical history: allergies, for which she takes Flonase.
Past surgical/trauma history: a stabbing trauma from falling on a rake while doing lawn work.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Positive for distal arm/wrist pain with wrist movement and mild swelling.
Neurological: Negative for numbness in the hand.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Musculoskeletal: Tenderness to palpation over the distal radius. Pain with bending the arm. Pain with stress and flexion of the thumb, which is the motion that mostly reproduces the pain. Less pain with backward movement (extension). Slight pain with flexion.

RESULTS
X-ray of the arm: No fractures and no abnormalities seen. Essentially normal.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Distal radius/forearm pain after striking the arm on a tennis net, most consistent with a muscle strain and possible contusion. No fracture on x-ray.
- Conservative treatment.
- Ice for pain and swelling.
- Motrin 800 mg three times a day with food as an anti-inflammatory.
- Patient to contact the office if not improved in about one week, and she will be reevaluated.
- Orders for procedures and medications to be placed as discussed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right-sided back pain and blood in the urine; kidney stone.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Anna is a patient referred by her primary care provider after being told she has a kidney stone. She reports right-sided back pain lasting about one week. The pain has moved down slightly to the right lower side and is pretty constant. She also noticed blood in her urine. She denies pain with urination. She took ibuprofen, which helped a little, but the pain persists. She reports mild nausea without vomiting. She had pain over the weekend (Easter break) and was seen by her provider this morning, who sent her here out of concern for a kidney stone. This is her first episode of kidney stones. Her father had kidney stones and may have passed a couple. She has probably not been drinking enough water.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever or chills.
GI: Mild nausea. No vomiting.
GU: Hematuria. No dysuria.
Musculoskeletal: Right back pain and right lower flank pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: No fever. Blood pressure and heart rate normal.
Abdomen: Mild tenderness to palpation. No rebound or guarding.
Back/Flank: Right CVA tenderness.

RESULTS
CT of the side: 0.5 cm stone in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right proximal ureteral kidney stone, 0.5 cm, without hydronephrosis. Exam shows right CVA tenderness.
- Push fluids, drinking as much as possible, to help pass the stone.
- Prescribe ibuprofen 800 mg as needed for pain.
- Provide a strainer to strain urine so the stone can be identified when it passes.
- Order BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture. Antibiotics will be decided based on urinalysis results if infection is present.
- Follow up in 1 to 2 weeks. If symptoms persist, discuss further treatment such as lithotripsy, a minimally invasive procedure using shock waves to break up the stone.
- Patient had no further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Shortness of breath and coughing up blood.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Dennis is a 57-year-old male with a history of diabetes, hypertension, and asthma who presents with shortness of breath for about two weeks. He wakes up short of breath. He gets short of breath when walking or exerting himself, and it recurs after he gets back home. He reports coughing up blood for about three weeks, estimated at three to four cups a day. He has had no vomiting of blood and no bleeding anywhere else. He has had no bruising or bleeding from the gums or teeth. He denies fevers. He has had chronic knee pain for quite some time without swelling. He denies leg or calf swelling and did not report recent travel. He has not been to the hospital or emergency room for this. He tried to get an office appointment but the office was booked.

Diabetes: He is on metformin 500 mg twice daily and wears a Dexcom. Glucose has been fluctuating for about a month, with post-meal spikes well over 200 and morning values around 150. The last hemoglobin A1c was about 7.7 (as recalled by the doctor), and diet and exercise improvements were previously discussed.

Hypertension: He takes Norvasc but has been skipping some days because his home blood pressure has been running low, sometimes in the lower 90s. Blood pressure in clinic today is about 120/70.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fevers.
Respiratory: Positive for shortness of breath and hemoptysis.
Cardiovascular: No leg or calf swelling reported.
Gastrointestinal: No vomiting of blood.
Musculoskeletal: Chronic knee pain without swelling.
Hematologic: No bruising or gum/teeth bleeding. No bleeding other than with cough.
Endocrine: Fluctuating blood glucose with elevated readings.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Pulse oximetry about 94%. Blood pressure about 120/70.
Neck: No JVD, no neck swelling, no carotid bruits.
Lungs: Rales and rhonchi, more on the right side. No wheezing. Diminished breath sounds on the right.
Cardiovascular: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from before. Otherwise regular rate and rhythm.
Abdomen: Soft.
Extremities: 1+ nonpitting edema of both ankles/lower extremities. No calf tenderness. Negative Homan sign.

RESULTS
Pulse oximetry about 94% in clinic. Prior hemoglobin A1c about 7.7 per the doctor's recollection. No other results available.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Shortness of breath with hemoptysis: Exam suggests a possible lung infection. The doctor is concerned about a blood clot or another serious process. Based on a BSA of 2.65, the minimum required resection by the Schnur scale is 1,792 grams, which should be attainable.

25-year-old female with symptomatic macromastia, presenting for evaluation of breast reduction. Nonsurgical treatments have given minimal relief. She is an ideal candidate for bilateral reduction mammoplasty. Given her extremely large breasts and the measurements, a nipple graft may be needed.

Plan:
- Photos will be taken today by Catherine. Symptom documentation is complete for the insurance submission.
- Submission to insurance for medical necessity approval will wait until her new plan begins, likely in July. The patient will notify the office with her new insurance information.

  - About 30% of patients cannot breastfeed afterward.
  - Breast size will change with weight gain, pregnancy, and hormones.
  - Nipple sensation is usually fine, but it may be altered or lost.
  - Some bruising is expected.
  - Back and neck pain relief is often almost immediate.

She took doxycycline twice daily for the first two weeks with significant improvement. Last week she reduced it to once daily, after the pharmacist reportedly advised limiting to once daily if improving. Since then the rash has plateaued and is no longer improving. She is not breastfeeding; she stopped breastfeeding before requesting doxycycline.

She did not use Elidel because she was worried after reading about it. The doctor explained that the concerns she read about apply to high-dose, long-term oral use after organ transplant, not to as-needed topical use.

Current regimen: sulfacetamide wash twice daily (not overly drying) and metronidazole cream applied immediately after washing. She uses no other lotions, Cetaphil cleanser, or wipes. She reports sun sensitivity and takes precautions, including wearing a hat. Insurance does not cover Elidel; the cost with a coupon was about $850. Eucrisa was also expensive, with prices fluctuating.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Skin: Residual facial rash. Denies dryness with the wash. Reports sun sensitivity.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Skin: Fitzpatrick skin type IV (to V). Bilateral medial cheeks with a few very faint erythematous papules. Mild redness around and underneath the nostrils.
Other exam findings: Use last visit exam where appropriate (per the doctor).

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Perioral dermatitis
2. Rosacea, including ocular rosacea

Improved but with a residual rash that plateaued after doxycycline was reduced to once daily.

Plan:
- Increase doxycycline to twice daily until the rash is gone, then once daily for another week, then stop. One refill remains. Counseled on GI upset/heartburn and photosensitivity (sunburn risk even if she does not usually burn); she is using sun protection. Doxycycline is low risk and will not be long-term.
- Start tacrolimus ointment (not a steroid; a calcineurin inhibitor) to the rash on the face twice daily until resolved, applied only to affected areas. Sent to Metro Market pharmacy. Counseled that a tingling, needle-like sensation or redness/flushing may occur 5-10 minutes after application, lasting seconds. It is not an allergy and she should continue using it as tolerated. It does not cause skin thinning. Stop tacrolimus once the rash resolves.
- Cancel Elidel cream (cost). Remove clindamycin from the medication list.
- Continue sulfacetamide wash (she may use twice daily if not dry, otherwise reduce to once daily) and metronidazole cream. Supply is sufficient.
- Add a basic moisturizer such as Vanicream, or petroleum jelly if very dry. Samples provided.
- Avoid steroids on the face, as they worsen this rash and can cause skin thinning. Avoid anti-aging and plant-based products. Hold off on restarting old products until the next visit, and discuss any new products with the doctor first.
- Ocular rosacea: gently wash eyelids once daily with a gentle cleanser such as Vanicream; use a Bruder mask as needed.
- If a mild flare occurs, use tacrolimus alone for a couple of days. If that is not enough, restart doxycycline as well.
- Patient instructions to be copied and pasted into her record.
- Follow-up in about 4 weeks. Call or send a MyChart message if the rash worsens.

She uses a walker now and becomes short of breath around the end of the driveway or around the cul-de-sac, particularly if she overdoes it. She says this is not very bothersome. She estimates her symptoms are about 70 to 80% of what they were six months ago, and she noticed nothing before that.

She has had severe leg pain for about one month and had a chest x-ray last week. She started taking pain pills for her legs. She feels overly tired, which she attributes to all of her medications.

She has lightheadedness and dizziness and takes a pill for it only when it gets bad, not daily. She denies syncope. She does not notice palpitations, racing heart, or skipped beats.

Her ankles have swelled for about six months, fluctuating and sometimes worse than other times. Her weight has gradually fallen over about a year, from her usual 130 pounds to 120 pounds now. She denies fevers and chills.

She is unsure whether she has ever had cardiac testing. She has had multiple prior surgeries, which were reviewed in her record and entered. She reports taking all medications reviewed with the clinic staff.

Family history: her son had a heart attack. Her brother had a stroke after developing diabetes. Her eldest sister had a heart problem. She says heart problems run in the family.

Social history: never smoker.

Allergies: no known drug allergies.

Medications mentioned: amlodipine, lisinopril, simvastatin 20 mg, levothyroxine, meclizine (as needed for dizziness), and pain pills for her legs.

Constitutional: Fatigue. Gradual weight loss of about 10 pounds over a year. No fevers or chills.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain, syncope, or palpitations. Ankle swelling present.
Respiratory: Exertional shortness of breath.
Musculoskeletal: Severe bilateral leg pain for about one month.
Neurologic: Lightheadedness and dizziness.

Constitutional: Elderly, in no acute distress.
Cardiovascular: Normal S1, and S2 is preserved. Normal rate and regular rhythm. 4/6 systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border with mild radiation to the carotids. She does not appear significantly volume overloaded.
Neurologic: Gait normal for age.
Blood pressure was noted to be good today (value not stated).

RESULTS
EKG today: Sinus rhythm with frequent PVCs and an anterior septal infarct pattern.
Outside records note diastolic dysfunction. She may have had an echocardiogram in the past.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Cardiac murmur, likely aortic stenosis
- 4/6 systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating mildly to the carotids.
- Her symptoms could be due to severe aortic stenosis, but the relatively preserved S2 is more consistent with moderate disease.
- Echocardiogram to be done today to assess cardiac structure, function, and the valve.
- Discussed that if the stenosis is severe, TAVR (transcatheter aortic valve replacement) may be considered. The patient is unsure she would want it given her age, and no decision is needed today.
- Surgical aortic valve replacement is not a good option because of her age and medical history.

2. PVCs
- The referral mentioned tachycardia. EKG shows sinus rhythm with frequent PVCs and an anterior septal infarct pattern.
- She has no significant palpitations and is asymptomatic.
- Start with the echocardiogram only. Depending on the results and the severity of aortic stenosis, consider an ischemic evaluation or a heart monitor to assess PVC burden.

- Managed by her PCP. She takes simvastatin 20 mg.
- She has bilateral leg pain, is of advanced age, and has no history of coronary artery disease, so the statin may be able to be stopped.
- This is to be discussed with her PCP. The echocardiogram results and recommendations will be sent to the PCP.

4. Lightheadedness and dizziness

- This may be related to aortic stenosis. PVCs could also contribute, though she feels no palpitations.
- Echocardiogram first, then consider a monitor.

5. Hypertension
- Blood pressure is good. Continue amlodipine and lisinopril unchanged.

6. Thyroid disease
- Continue levothyroxine unchanged. (The doctor called this hyperthyroidism, though she is on levothyroxine.)

She came home one day with sudden-onset right-sided abdominal pain, bent over in pain. Her family suspected appendicitis. She was still vomiting and in significant pain, so she was taken to Jacksonville, where she was told the right kidney was atrophic, much smaller than the other, and likely not functioning. Imaging there also reportedly showed cysts on the kidney, ovaries, and possibly other sites, swollen lymph nodes, and infection. She did not improve over 1-2 days, and the family came to Atlanta, where she stayed about four days and was treated. She improved afterward and has had no further vomiting, but she continues to complain of abdominal pain and burning, especially when eating. Currently she reports mild abdominal pain and burning. She sometimes has difficulty starting urination. No blood in urine noticed. Her mother reports burning with urination after certain drinks such as soda, so she drinks only Gatorade or water.

Past history: Previously healthy. It was suggested she may have had a severe infection that affected her kidney. At age 4 she was hospitalized 3-4 times, sometimes for 3 days, with recurrent fevers and symptoms treated with fluids and antibiotics, without a source identified. This recurred over a couple of months and then stopped. Her doctor suspects kidney problems since then. No pregnancy or delivery complications. She has seen GI and genetics; the genetic panel showed no clinically significant mutations.

Medications: Pepcid 40 mg daily; Claritin for allergies.

Family history: Father had a renal transplant for obstructive uropathy (congenital, not caught in time) and died at 47 of a massive heart attack. Father's sister (great aunt) had end-stage renal disease, CKD stage 5, diabetes, and hypertension as an adult. Cousins have kidney issues. Mother had breast cancer. (Note: at the end of the visit, the doctor's dictation of a family member's record was unclear and discussed with the family; the discussion about whether the death was from the heart attack or occurred while on dialysis was not resolved, and details of that record are uncertain.)

Social: Active in softball and hopes to join the drill team over the summer. Family tries to eat well.

Respiratory: Lungs sound normal.
Remainder of exam within normal limits.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
14-year-old female with an atrophic right kidney and compensatory enlargement of the left kidney. Kidney function and blood pressure are currently normal. She is at higher risk of hypertension and proteinuria. No intervention is needed today.

- Annual monitoring: renal ultrasound for kidney size and function, urinalysis for protein and blood, and blood pressure check.
- Avoid NSAIDs such as ibuprofen; use Tylenol instead.
- Maintain hydration, especially during sports, with at least 2 liters of water per day, to avoid dehydration.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Michelle King is a 39-year-old female with quadriplegia due to a prior spinal cord injury and a suprapubic catheter. She was admitted on 06/29/2021 with increasing spasms, lightheadedness, significant constipation, and diaphoresis. In the ED she was febrile with a white blood cell count of 23,000. There was concern for ongoing urinary tract infection, and she was treated with IV antibiotics. She also had labile blood pressure, headache, and vomiting. She improved slowly and was discharged after clinical improvement. Cultures were obtained and reviewed.

The patient does not believe this was a UTI. She believes she was constipated and that this caused her high blood pressure (autonomic dysreflexia). She reports she had hardly any bowel movements in the hospital, then had a large bowel movement at home and felt much better. She told the hospital team this on admission. They obtained x-rays, but no CT was done, and the team did not think constipation was the cause. She went to the ER because her blood pressure was out of control, causing headache and vomiting, and she had exhausted what she could do at home. She reports she had not had a regular bowel movement in a while despite taking MiraLAX daily, and she doubles the dose when she does not go. She has lactulose, which takes about two days to work and which she describes as a rough two days. She feels back to her normal self and otherwise is doing well. She denies pain or discomfort. Weather in the weeks before admission was very hot and humid, and she tends to stay indoors when it is hot.

The patient is unvaccinated for COVID-19. Her concerns are unknown long-term side effects and reports of "vaccine injury." She feels she is young and healthy enough to beat COVID-19 even with limited respiratory function. She takes vitamin C and multivitamins and is closely monitored. She does not get an annual flu shot. She says she is open-minded.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Reports feeling back to her normal self. Fever and diaphoresis were present during the admission.
Gastrointestinal: Constipation prior to admission, with vomiting during the acute episode. Improved after a large bowel movement at home.
Neurological: Headache and lightheadedness during the acute episode, now resolved. Spasms prior to admission.
Musculoskeletal: Denies pain or discomfort currently.
Cardiovascular: High, labile blood pressure during the acute episode.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Lung auscultation was performed during deep breathing. No findings were stated.

RESULTS
Per the hospital course: WBC 23,000 in the ED. Urine cultures were reviewed and were not impressive. Abdominal x-rays were done during admission; no CT was performed. Per the doctor, the patient's white count has been mildly elevated at times, and it was normal last year.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute on chronic constipation, with leukocytosis and recent hospitalization
- The patient believes the hospitalization was more likely due to autonomic dysreflexia from her quadriplegia, triggered by constipation, and less likely a true UTI. She had significant vital sign changes, including blood pressure fluctuations.
- Urine cultures were unimpressive. Leukocytosis may be related to inflammation from constipation. Heat and dehydration may have worsened constipation.
- She has a good bowel regimen: MiraLAX regularly as primary treatment and lactulose as rescue for severe constipation.
- Plan: return in 2 to 3 weeks (the doctor also mentioned 3 to 4 weeks) for updated fasting labs including a repeat CBC to confirm the white count trends down, plus a full cholesterol panel since she is due. If the white count remains elevated, further evaluation of her bowels would be considered.

2. Quadriplegia
- Prior spinal cord injury with a suprapubic catheter. No additional plan was discussed.

3. COVID-19 vaccine status
- She is unvaccinated and hesitant. The doctor recommended vaccination, considers her high risk given her quadriplegia and limited respiratory function, and believes the vaccine is safe, with rare potential side effects such as Guillain-Barré syndrome.
- The doctor advised that vaccination is the only true preventive mechanism and does not believe supplements will help prevent COVID-19.
- The patient was encouraged to consider vaccination and to ask any further questions. The decision is hers.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right index finger pain and stiffness after a motor vehicle accident; seeking a second opinion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip Gutierrez is a 50-year-old right-handed male (DOB 1/12/71) who works as an x-ray tech. He presents for a second opinion regarding his right index finger. In March of this year (about 3 months ago) he was a passenger in a car that was rear-ended multiple times. He felt two bumps that slung him forward and stretched out his right index finger. He felt as if he had laid on the finger and it went backward. The finger has hurt and remained swollen since the accident. He cannot make a fist, the pain is sometimes unbearable, and even driving hurts.

He was seen at an orthopedic practice, largely by the physical therapy staff and a PA, and was sent to occupational therapy. He was previously offered an injection but declined steroid because of a reaction to dexamethasone that causes his heart to race. He was scheduled to see Dr. Alice Davis but does not appear to have done so. An MRI was obtained for concern about a capsular strain with or without rupture of the FDS tendon. The patient understood that the MRI showed a tear and that the prior orthopedist would not inject because it could worsen the tear, and also did not want to do surgery. He was also told not to keep rubbing the finger or using the hand. He feels he is not getting medical care. Occupational therapy maneuvers to straighten the finger caused pain after he left and swelling of the whole finger. He bought a splint, thinking it would straighten the finger. He has no therapy currently scheduled.

PMH: No diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis.
Medications: A blood pressure pill, otherwise no chronic medications.
Allergies/reactions: Dexamethasone (heart racing). Itching with methylprednisolone.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right index finger pain, swelling, and stiffness; unable to make a fist.
Neurological: Slight numbness of the finger noted during the exam.
Cardiovascular: Heart racing with dexamethasone (historical).
Skin: Itching with methylprednisolone (historical).
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Very pleasant, cooperative, healthy male in no distress.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. 2+ radial pulse.
Right hand: No swelling or bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases, slightly diminished over the PIP of the index finger compared to the middle finger. The index finger rests in about 10 degrees of PIP flexion. Pain when the finger is pushed to correct the posture, less painful at an adjacent site, with a feeling of slight numbness. Pain described as a tearing sensation with maximal flexion of the fingertip. Pain with passive flexion at the MCP joint, felt to be from stretching due to prolonged lack of motion. Extensors and collateral ligaments are intact per the doctor's assessment.

RESULTS
MRI right index finger (4/24/2021, outside orthopedic practice): Focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint. Partial-thickness tear of the right FDS. Fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint intact, as is the MCP joint capsule. Extensor tendons intact.

X-rays, 4 views of the right hand (today): No bony abnormalities. Joint congruency throughout all lesser digits. No concerning soft tissue shadows. No arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Post-traumatic, rather severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger, with a partial tear of one half of the FDS tendon. The FDP, which goes to the fingertip, is intact. There is significant scar tissue and inflammation around the FDS tendon, blocking excursion of the other tendons so they cannot get through to the pulley. The finger is stiff and sore, with intact collateral ligaments and extensors.

Plan:
1. Steroid injection (trigger finger injection) into the right flexor tendon sheath using betamethasone (Celestone), avoiding dexamethasone and methylprednisolone given prior reactions. Planned dose 1 cc of Celestone with 0.5 cc lidocaine. The patient expects relief in about 3 to 5 days and further improvement over the next couple of weeks. The injection may need to be repeated.
2. Procedure note: The first attempt was stopped because of a dramatic, violent painful reaction to needle introduction, with contortion and withdrawal of the hand, raising concern for a needle stick. The needle was withdrawn. The patient was counseled on the importance of getting therapeutic steroid into the flexor tendon sheath. A second attempt was made with the same technique using 1 cc Celestone and 0.5 cc lidocaine. A small palmar vein bled a scant amount, which was cleaned and covered with a Band-Aid. The patient was reassured repeatedly that no harm was done to the finger.
3. Ice the finger this evening and take ibuprofen.
4. The patient must actively move and bend the finger. He will not tear anything or break a bone. A splint immobilizes and does not help.
5. Outpatient therapy prescription: once a week for 6 weeks, at the prior therapy location. The goal is full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions. Weekly check-ins provide accountability.
6. It is safe to drive after the injection.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Matthew is a patient with a history of hypertension who presents with vision changes in the right eye. He reports trouble adjusting to dark, dim environments, especially when dining out at restaurants. He also has decreased vision when reading in dark places. He reports that straight lines appear crooked or wavy, for example door frames and the grooves in the paneling in his office. Symptoms have been present for a while and have worsened over the last 3 to 4 months.

He smokes about a pack of cigarettes per day. He has tried hypnosis, lozenges, and chewing gum and gets close to quitting, but relapses when he is out without his wife and buys a cigarette from someone.

He has a history of high blood pressure. He admits he has not taken his blood pressure medication for a while; the bottle is in the back corner of a cupboard and he forgets to take it. Home blood pressure monitoring was not described.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Eyes: Decreased vision in dim light and when reading in the dark. Distortion of straight lines (metamorphopsia) in the right eye.
All other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Eyes:
- Anterior segment: Posterior chamber intraocular lenses in both eyes.
- Right eye: Cornea clear. No NVI. Cup-to-disc ratio 0.2. Retina attached 360 degrees with no holes or tears. RPE changes in the fovea. Posterior segment shows drusen in the macula, retinal thickening, subretinal fluid and exudate accumulation, and positive for hemorrhage.
- Left eye: Cornea clear. No NVI. Cup-to-disc ratio 0.3. RPE changes in the fovea. No hemorrhage or subretinal fluid. Retina attached.

- OCT: Drusen deposits under the retinal pigment epithelium, subretinal fluid accumulation, and choroidal neovascular membrane visualized.
- Fluorescein angiography: Focal area of leakage in the right eye, consistent with neovascular age-related macular degeneration.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration, right eye.
- Exam, OCT, and fluorescein angiography are consistent with the diagnosis. The disease has advanced to a stage that usually leads to more severe vision loss.
- Explained that abnormal blood vessels grow beneath the retina and leak fluid and blood, creating a central blind spot. It is the most common cause of severe vision loss.
- Plan: Monthly intravitreal injections of Lucentis after the eye is numbed. The patient was told he should not feel pain with the injection.
- Counseled that injections over time can slow the rate of vision decline and may even stop it, though some small vision loss may still occur. This is the best chance of maintaining vision.
- The patient had no questions. The nurse will prep him and the first injection will be done today.

2. Tobacco use, about 1 pack per day.
- Counseled on the importance of cutting back or quitting altogether.

3. Hypertension, medication nonadherence.
- Counseled on taking blood pressure medication as prescribed, starting today.
- Suggested placing the pill bottle on the counter as a reminder.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for adult hydrocephalus, first visit after shunt surgery.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Watson is an 86-year-old male (DOB 04/12/1934) who returns for follow-up of adult hydrocephalus. He has been followed since May 2020, when he presented with 8 to 10 years of progressive gait impairment, cognitive impairment, and decreased bladder control. The diagnosis of adult hydrocephalus was established with a spinal catheter protocol in June 2020. He underwent shunt surgery on August 1, 2020, with placement of a Medtronic Strata programmable ventriculoperitoneal shunt programmed at level 2.0. This is his first visit since surgery, about three months ago. He is accompanied by his daughter, Theresa.

He has not been sick or hospitalized since surgery. His daughter reports he has been doing much better.

Gait: Walking has improved. He can now walk to the dining room, which he could not do before surgery. He still has times when he needs help.

Bladder: Control improved somewhat after surgery but has since leveled off. He wears diapers. No skin sores from the diapers, and no decreased or painful urination.

Cognition: The patient feels better and no longer feels lost when talking to someone. His daughter relays that another daughter, Hannah, said she feels she can have a normal conversation with him again.

He denies headaches, pain at the shunt site, and abdominal pain.

The patient asked whether he will be able to drive again.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for impaired ability to carry out daily functions. Negative for fever or unintentional weight loss.
GU: Positive for urinary incontinence and wearing a diaper. Negative for genital sores, decreased urine output, or painful urination.
Neurological: Positive for continued walking impairment and cognitive impairment. Negative for headaches, recent falls, or hallucinations.
Psychiatric: Negative for depression, excessive worrying, or mood swings.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 124/80, HR 64, RR 18, weight 174 lb, pain 0/10.
General: Pleasant and cooperative. Converses easily, with his daughter adding some details.
Shunt: Site clean, dry, and intact. Setting confirmed at 2.
Neurological/Cognitive: Tested for recent and remote memory, attention span, concentration, and fund of knowledge. MMSE 26/30 with spelling and 25/30 with calculations. He recalled two of three memory words with cuing and the third with multiple choice. Initial scores were 24/30 with spelling and 23/30 with calculations, and at that time he recalled no memory words with cuing and only one with multiple choice.
Gait: Tinetti assessment without an assistive device. Gait score 6 to 8/12, balance score 12/16, total 18 to 20/28. Initial total was 15 to 17/28.
Cranial nerves: Pupils equal. EOMs intact. Face symmetric. No dysarthria.
Motor: Normal bulk and strength.
Coordination: Slow on finger-to-nose.

RESULTS
CT head 10/15/2020: Frontal horn span at the level of the foramen of Monro is 4.6 cm. Third ventricular contour is flat with a span of 10 mm. By the doctor's reading, there is a tiny amount of blood in the right frontal/parietal region with a tiny subdural fluid collection. This was not noted by the radiologist, who reported no extra-axial fluid collections. There is also substantial small vessel ischemic change.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Adult hydrocephalus, status post VP shunt placement
2. Gait impairment
3. Urinary incontinence and urgency
4. Cognitive impairment

Mr. Watson has improved since shunt surgery in gait, cognition, and, to a lesser degree, bladder control. MMSE and Tinetti scores are slightly improved from baseline. CT shows a tiny possible right-sided blood/fluid collection that the doctor does not believe is causing symptoms. He has no headaches or pain and has improved clinically.

Plan:
- Leave the shunt set at 2.0 for another 2 to 3 months before considering any change.
- Follow up in 3 months. The family will schedule at the front desk.
- Driving: It is unlikely his movement speed will improve enough to pass the driver safety evaluation now. Some patients improve over 9 to 12 months, and the doctor would consider recommending evaluation if he improves. He may enroll in a driver safety program without a recommendation and continue to be monitored for improvement.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left shoulder pain for a few weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Betty is a patient who reports left shoulder pain for the past three weeks. She cannot identify a specific inciting event. She is very active and has been renovating her basement. She denies any trauma, including falls or hitting the shoulder. She has had occasional aches and pains in the past that were managed with Tylenol, but no prior pain specifically in this shoulder is described. The pain is isolated to the left shoulder.

Reaching for or lifting objects causes significant pain, and she avoids raising her arm overhead because of pain. The pain is constant. It worsens with pressure, particularly when lying on the left side. She is a side sleeper and has difficulty sleeping because of discomfort. The pain is present when lying on her back as well, but increases when she lies directly on the shoulder.

She takes two extra-strength Tylenol every six to eight hours, which helps take the edge off. Pain is 7/10 without Tylenol and 2-3/10 with Tylenol. She denies numbness or tingling in the arm or hand.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Positive for left shoulder pain with limited use of the arm and difficulty sleeping on the left side.
Neurological: Negative for numbness or tingling in the arm or hand.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Reviewed by the physician; reported as good.
Left shoulder: Limited active and passive range of motion. Tenderness over the greater tuberosity of the humerus. No tenderness at the sternoclavicular or clavicular joints.
Hands: Good grip strength bilaterally.
Neurovascular, left arm: Capillary refill brisk, less than 3 seconds. Motor and sensation intact to light touch.

RESULTS
X-ray of the left shoulder: No fracture or bony abnormality.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left shoulder pain, most likely due to rotator cuff tendinopathy. The physician explained that this represents injury to the tendons that make up or attach to the shoulder muscles.
- Order MRI of the left shoulder to ensure nothing else is going on.
- Refer to physical therapy for approximately 6-8 weeks.
- Continue Tylenol as needed.
- If symptoms do not improve, consider a steroid injection of the left shoulder.
- The patient asked whether the pain will go away. The physician expressed belief that it will, noting that many patients do well with physical therapy, and plans a conservative approach initially.
- Follow-up in about two weeks. The nurse will provide paperwork.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hypertension and palpitations. New patient visit following a recent emergency room visit.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jordan Roberts is a 49-year-old man (DOB 3/2/1972) with hypertension and palpitations. He was recently seen in the emergency room, around March, for high blood pressure and palpitations. He had had a few cups of coffee and no breakfast that day and thinks it was more likely a panic attack. He has not had a recurrence of the palpitations since.

He reports blood pressure problems since he was young, and a lot of his family has high blood pressure. A new primary doctor started him on a combination medication (Benicar HCT 40-25, which contains hydrochlorothiazide) about a month ago. He continues to take amlodipine 10 mg daily. He checks his blood pressure at home every morning on waking, and readings have been running about 146 to 155. He is not yet in the 120s. He is trying to reduce his salt intake and feels he is doing well with it. He walks on the treadmill when he can. His potassium one week ago was 4.0 and has not been rechecked since.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Cardiovascular: No recurrence of palpitations since the ER visit.
Gastrointestinal: No abdominal tenderness with palpation.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds good.
Respiratory: Lungs sound good.
Abdomen: No tenderness on palpation.
Extremities: Ankles and feet examined for swelling; no swelling, all looks good.

RESULTS
Potassium one week ago: 4.0.
Thyroid profile from March 1, 2021 was requested to be copied forward; no values were discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Resistant hypertension. He is on three medications (amlodipine 10 mg, olmesartan/hydrochlorothiazide 40-25) at maximum doses, and blood pressure is still not at goal. The doctor discussed possible secondary drivers such as hyperaldosteronism and parathyroid abnormalities.

1. Start spironolactone.
2. Counseling on risks of spironolactone with hydrochlorothiazide: electrolyte disturbance, dehydration (stay hydrated; dizziness on standing suggests dehydration), hyperkalemia (rare; baseline potassium 4.0 leaves room), and low sodium. Dizziness is also possible. Gynecomastia occurs in about 1 in 100 men; if it happens, stop the medication and notify the doctor. The patient understood and agreed to the plan.
3. Metabolic panel and blood pressure check in two weeks, with follow-up in two weeks.
4. If not controlled on spironolactone, refer to the resistant hypertension clinic to evaluate for secondary causes and consider procedures such as renal denervation, which has been shown to lower blood pressure by about 10 points but carries risks, so not everyone is a candidate. The next medication would be carvedilol, which the doctor tries to avoid because of the potential for erectile dysfunction. This was discussed with the patient.
5. Lifestyle: Provided information on the DASH eating plan. Keep salt under 2000 mg per day (recommendation is 1500 mg). Increase potassium. Treadmill about 30 minutes most days could lower blood pressure by 7 to 10 points. Reviewed the American Heart Association website, heart.org.
6. Counseled that uncontrolled hypertension at a young age can lead to an enlarged heart, heart failure, kidney failure, and stroke. The patient verbalized understanding.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left back pain from a suspected kidney stone. Follow-up of hypertension and diabetes.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Linda has a past medical history of hypertension, diabetes, and recurrent kidney stones. She presents with 3 days of constant left back pain that has since moved lower, toward the groin. She cannot get comfortable. She is able to urinate, but this morning she noticed blood in her urine. She has had some chills and mild nausea, and she cannot eat because of the pain. She denies fever. She believes this is her third kidney stone episode, and her last one was a while ago. Previous stones took about 3-4 days to pass, and she has not passed this one yet. She has taken Tylenol and ibuprofen without relief. She was previously advised to be careful with ibuprofen because of her blood pressure but has used it because of the severity of the pain.

Hypertension: She is on Norvasc 2.5 mg. She obtained a home blood pressure cuff but has not been consistent in checking it. Systolic readings are usually in the 130s, sometimes in the 140s, and once reached 150. Diastolic readings are 70-80. Her blood pressure was in the 180s at diagnosis. She is trying to limit sodium to 2,300 mg per day but has difficulty because she likes french fries. She would like help with her diet.

Diabetes: She is on metformin 500 mg and takes it daily. She checks her blood sugar before meals daily, and readings are in the low 100s. Her last A1c was 7.3. A glucose test a couple of months ago was around 300.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for chills. Negative for fever.
Cardiovascular: Negative for chest pain.
Gastrointestinal: Positive for nausea and decreased appetite. Negative for abdominal pain.
Genitourinary: Positive for hematuria. Positive for left back pain radiating toward the groin.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously known.
Respiratory: Lungs clear bilaterally with no crackles or wheezes.
Abdomen: Tenderness to palpation. No rebound or guarding.
Back/Flank: CVA tenderness on palpation. The transcript states right-sided, although the patient's pain is on the left. Back is painful to palpation.
Vitals: Blood pressure was noted to be a little high at today's visit, attributed to pain.

RESULTS
Previous A1c 7.3. Glucose approximately 300 a couple of months ago. No new results from today's visit.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Kidney stone, recurrent (third episode), with CVA tenderness suggesting inflammation around the kidney.
- Oxycodone 5 mg every 6-8 hours as needed for pain.
- Continue Tylenol for breakthrough pain.
- Push fluids.
- Strain urine to catch the stone.
- Refer to urology, to be seen even if the stone passes, given recurrent stones and the goal of preventing future episodes.

2. Hypertension.
- Continue Norvasc 2.5 mg. Home readings are acceptable, so no changes.
- Continue home blood pressure monitoring, at least three times a week.
- Limit sodium to 2,300 mg per day.
- Referral to a dietitian for diet support.

3. Diabetes.
- Continue metformin 500 mg daily.
- Referral to nutrition/dietitian. The goal is that with dietary changes she may eventually come off both medications.

The patient verbalized understanding and agreement with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for chronic congestive heart failure with diastolic dysfunction. Pre-operative planning for right knee replacement.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Nicole Miller is a patient (DOB 09/18/1949) with chronic congestive heart failure with diastolic dysfunction, seen for follow-up. She had increasing dyspnea in the spring. The heart failure marker was about 3,000 in March and rose to about 6,000 in April. Furosemide was changed to torsemide 20 mg by mouth daily. Lisinopril was increased to 10 mg daily in March. She is not currently on a potassium supplement. At the last visit in April, she expressed interest in right knee replacement this summer at East Metro, and it was recommended that her cardiovascular status be optimized beforehand. Surgery is scheduled for the 24th.

Since the last visit she has lost about 3 to 3.5 pounds. She reports that her urinary urgency is much improved, and she attributes this to oxybutynin. She had leg cramps in both legs after falling asleep with a ceiling fan on, which she thought was from being cold. She drank about 4 ounces of pickle juice and the cramps resolved. She is still taking an iron supplement and reports bowel movements are fine. Her heartburn was bad for a while. She took Prilosec for about two weeks in January, stopped her other medication during that time, then returned to her stomach medication and has had no problems since. She is due for a colonoscopy. She has Medicare and private insurance (through her husband), and the husband's insurance may be ending soon, so she would like the colonoscopy done within 30 days. She is on clopidogrel.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: Dyspnea earlier in the spring, now improved.
Genitourinary: Urinary urgency much improved.
Gastrointestinal: Heartburn resolved. Bowel movements normal.
Musculoskeletal: Recent bilateral leg cramps, resolved.
Constitutional: Weight loss of about 3 to 3.5 pounds.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Breathing is non-labored. Lungs sound good on auscultation with deep breaths. Blood pressure is looking good. The doctor used the general physical exam template. Weight is down about 3 to 3.5 pounds since April.

RESULTS
- Hemoglobin: still doing well (history of anemia).
- Potassium: 3.9, stable on torsemide.
- Creatinine: 0.7 (previously 0.8).
- BUN: 23, slightly elevated.
- Magnesium: 1.7, a little under the goal of about 2.
- Random (non-fasting) glucose: 169.
- Prior A1c: 5.5 in March. The assessment also mentions an A1c of 5.1 on the last check.
- Heart failure marker: about 3,000 in March and about 6,000 in April. Current result is pending.
- EKG: to be repeated today.
- Chest x-ray: done recently, so not needed again.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Chronic congestive heart failure with diastolic dysfunction (mixed presentation). She had an exacerbation earlier in the spring and was switched from furosemide to torsemide. She is symptomatically much better, down about 3 to 3.5 pounds, and breathing is non-labored. Creatinine is appropriate and she is tolerating the current torsemide dose.
- Repeat EKG today.
- Continue the current regimen.
- Follow up on the pending heart failure marker.
- Magnesium is 1.7. Recommend a magnesium supplement twice daily, aiming for a level around 2 to help stabilize the heart muscle.

2. Pre-operative evaluation for right knee replacement (scheduled for the 24th, end of June).
- Hold clopidogrel for one week before surgery. The patient has reminders written on her phone and a letter by her bed, and the office will also remind her.
- Complete a pre-op check within two weeks of surgery, during the first or second week of June.
- Repeat EKG may be needed before surgery and will be done today.
- No chest x-ray or additional blood work is needed, since both were done recently.
- Random glucose may need to be repeated for pre-op.

3. Colon cancer screening (overdue). There is no family history of colon cancer.
- Place the referral now for a screening colonoscopy within the next 30 days, before her insurance changes. Options are Dr. Martin at County Surgical Services or Valley Medical at Springfield. The doctor will call around to find the earliest availability.
- Completing the colonoscopy should not delay the knee surgery.

4. Diabetes.
- No A1c is needed today. She may need another before surgery next month.

5. Leg cramps. Advised to keep pickle juice in moderation because of its salt content.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hospital follow-up after an acute on chronic congestive heart failure exacerbation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is an 82-year-old male with a past medical history of hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease who presents for hospital follow-up after an acute on chronic CHF exacerbation.

Before admission, he noticed ankle swelling despite trying to watch his diet. One day he became very short of breath and called 911. Paramedics placed him on a mask for breathing support. In the ER, his blood pressure was reported as very high (200/90). He admits to occasionally missing a dose or two of his medications, though he tries to take them. He also admits to dietary indiscretion, particularly pizza and chicken wings at weekend parties with friends.

He was hospitalized for a couple of days. He received a medication that caused significant urination and IV diuretic therapy, and he believes his blood pressure medications were changed. He feels much better now. Since discharge he has been following his diet and taking his medications because he does not want to return to the hospital. He bought a home blood pressure cuff, which arrived last week, and checks his blood pressure about every other day. He reports readings have been good. He denies shortness of breath, trouble sleeping, and chest pain since returning home. He can move around without difficulty and takes an afternoon nap.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain. Reports prior ankle swelling.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath since discharge.
Neurologic/Sleep: Denies problems sleeping.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: BP 128/72, heart rate 79, respiratory rate 26 (doctor attributed this to talking), O2 saturation 99%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Cardiovascular: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously noted and stable.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram: Preserved EF of 55%, abnormal diastolic filling, mild to moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive heart failure (recent acute on chronic exacerbation): Likely caused by dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension.
- Continue Bumex 2 mg daily.
- Continue dietary monitoring and avoid salty foods. Counseled to cut back on pizza and chicken wings.
- Weigh daily and call if he gains 3 pounds in 2 days.
- Refer to a nutritionist for diet education.
- Continue monitoring the stable murmur.

2. Hypertension:
- Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily.
- Continue Norvasc 5 mg once daily.
- Order a renal artery ultrasound to rule out secondary causes.
- Counseled on consistent medication adherence.
- Continue home blood pressure monitoring.

3. Stage 3 chronic kidney disease:
- Order additional labs to ensure he tolerates the current regimen.

Follow-up in 3 months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Uncontrolled hypertension. Referred by PCP for evaluation of persistently high blood pressure and abnormal kidney findings on recent blood work.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Virginia is a patient who established care with a new PCP last year. Her PCP has made several medication changes and added two blood pressure medications after noting elevated blood pressure. The patient reports she is now taking her medications consistently, though she was not adherent previously. Blood pressure remains difficult to control. Her PCP also noted something regarding her kidneys on her last blood work, and referred her here.

Most days she feels fine and remains busy at work, but she can tell when her blood pressure is high. She checks her blood pressure at home a few times a week with an electronic arm cuff. Readings have been rising, with a recent high of 170/90. She called her PCP, who increased her medications again. She has noticed that the CVS blood pressure machine was no longer available since the pandemic; the doctor believes the CVS on Main Street may have brought it back.

Diet: She acknowledges her diet could be better. She eats pizza, wings, and subs, especially during football season, and tries to cut down on non-game days.

Mild headaches occur only when blood pressure is very high. No chest pain, no shortness of breath, including with exertion. Mild lower extremity swelling after prolonged standing, otherwise none.

Current medications: amlodipine (Norvasc) 10 mg daily and carvedilol 25 mg twice daily. She was previously on lisinopril, which was adjusted. She takes NSAIDs (Advil, Motrin, Aleve) occasionally for knee or back pain, not daily.

Alcohol: a couple of beers during the week and one or two on the weekends.

Family history: both parents have hypertension, and one parent had kidney disease.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Feels fine most days.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain. Mild lower extremity swelling after prolonged standing.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath, including with exertion.
Neurological: Mild headaches only when blood pressure is very high.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 169/74, HR 88, oxygen saturation 98%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Lungs: Clear.
Cardiovascular: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur.
Extremities: 1+ pitting edema bilaterally.

RESULTS
Recent blood work from PCP reportedly noted a kidney abnormality; no values were discussed.
Home BP: up to 170/90.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Uncontrolled hypertension. Likely multifactorial. Workup for a secondary cause before further medication changes:
- Renal artery ultrasound to evaluate for renal artery stenosis.
- Morning aldosterone and renin levels.
- Urine collection and 24-hour urine collection to evaluate for adrenal causes.
- Start doxazosin (Cardura) 4 mg once daily.
- Continue amlodipine 10 mg daily and carvedilol 25 mg twice daily.
- Decrease alcohol to one to two drinks per week.
- Decrease salt intake substantially. Referral to a nutritionist.
- Stop NSAIDs (Advil, Motrin, Aleve). Use Tylenol only for pain.
- Record home blood pressures at the same time each day for the next 3 weeks and bring the log to the next visit. Check whether the Main Street CVS has a blood pressure machine available.
- Follow up in 3 weeks.
- The doctor will communicate the plan to the PCP.

2. Systolic ejection murmur, 2/6. Needs additional evaluation; the doctor stated it requires a closer look.

3. Bilateral 1+ pitting lower extremity edema. Noted on exam.

4. Abnormal kidney findings on recent blood work, per PCP. Being evaluated as part of the workup above.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for coronary artery disease after myocardial infarction with stent placement. Patient also reports dizziness on standing and feeling down.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male seen for follow-up approximately 3 to 4 months after his last visit. He had a heart attack about 6 months ago with a stent placed in the left anterior descending artery. He reports he is doing okay and feels the medications are helping, though he is concerned about the number of medications he takes. He continues aspirin, Brilinta, and fish oil. He is also taking Crestor and metoprolol 50 mg once daily. He previously worried Crestor might cause muscle aches; no muscle aches were reported at this visit.

His only physical complaint is dizziness when he stands up quickly. He is unsure whether it is related to the heart attack or the medication.

He asked about the stent duration and was counseled that stents are permanent. He was told to report any recurrence of chest pain or exertional shortness of breath.

He has diabetes and was previously asked to follow up with a dietitian but forgot with whom he was to follow up. He reports fasting glucose around 130 and a recent hemoglobin A1c that he thought was close to 16. He has a fondness for sweets, including chocolate chip cookies. He had a recent blood test after receiving contrast dye.

He has stage 3 chronic kidney disease. His last nephrology visit was probably a year ago. He has discarded Motrin and Advil. He asked what he can take for headaches.

He reports feeling down since his heart attack. He denies thoughts of harming himself or others. He lives alone with his dog and finds it lonely. He is retiring and has plenty of time. He asked about medication for his mood. He needs medication refills.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Neurological: Dizziness on rapid standing. Headaches mentioned (taking no NSAIDs).
Psychiatric: Feeling down since heart attack, loneliness. Denies thoughts of harming self or others.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain or shortness of breath reported.
Musculoskeletal: No muscle aches reported.
Extremities: Acknowledges leg puffiness.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure about 127/80. Vital signs described as good.
Neck: No jugular venous distention or carotid bruits.
Cardiac: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left base, previously heard.
Extremities: 1+ nonpitting edema in the lower extremities. No evidence of fluid retention otherwise.

RESULTS
Kidney function (creatinine) is stable after contrast dye exposure. Patient-reported hemoglobin A1c close to 16 (goal about 6) and fasting glucose about 130.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Coronary artery disease, status post MI with LAD stent about 6 months ago. Doing well.
- Continue aspirin for life. Continue Brilinta for another 6 months. Continue fish oil.
- Refer to cardiac rehab.
- Refill metoprolol, Crestor 40 mg once daily, and aspirin.
- No stress test needed at this time. Patient to report chest pain or exertional shortness of breath.
- Dizziness on standing is likely related to the beta-blocker (metoprolol) as the body adjusts. Counseled on rising slowly.
- Mild leg edema may be medication related.
- Continue diet modification.

2. Stage 3 chronic kidney disease. Kidney function stable after contrast.
- Contact Dr. Miller (nephrology) to arrange an appointment.
- Continue avoiding NSAIDs such as Motrin and Advil. Tylenol is acceptable for headaches.

3. Diabetes, with markedly elevated A1c by patient report.
- Repeat hemoglobin A1c.
- Referral for dietitian/diabetic education.
- Doctor will speak with the primary care physician about the insulin regimen.

4. Low mood and difficulty adjusting after heart attack, possible mild depression. No suicidal or homicidal ideation.
- Referral to psychiatry.

5. Medication refills to be sent to the patient's pharmacy of choice.
